notes.front: What four dimensions define software architecture (Richards & Ford)?
notes.back:
• Structure — the architecture style(s) in use (layered, microservices, …).
  • Architecture characteristics — the “-ilities” the system must support.
  • Architecture decisions — hard rules for how the system is built.
  • Design principles — guidelines (not hard rules) for building it.
“Everything in software architecture is a tradeoff.” Corollary: if you think you’ve found something that isn’t a tradeoff, you just haven’t identified the tradeoff yet.
“Why is more important than how.” Knowing why a decision was made is more valuable than knowing how it was implemented.

A decision is a hard rule that must be followed (e.g. “all inter-layer calls go through the business layer”). A principle is a guideline that leaves implementation latitude (e.g. “prefer asynchronous messaging where practical”).

notes.front: The 8 core expectations of a software architect?
notes.back:
• Make architecture decisions
  • Continually analyze the architecture
  • Keep current with trends
  • Ensure compliance with decisions
  • Have diverse exposure / experience
  • Have business-domain knowledge
  • Possess interpersonal skills
  • Understand and navigate politics

notes.front: The knowledge “triangle” — how should an architect balance breadth vs depth?
notes.back: Knowledge splits into: stuff you know, stuff you know you don’t know, and stuff you don’t know you don’t know. Developers maximise depth (stuff you know); architects should favour breadth — a large “know you don’t know” zone — since broad exposure supports better decisions than deep but narrow expertise.

An architect who irrationally fixates on a past bad experience and reverts to an unlikely worst-case worry on every decision. The fix is to assess risk realistically per situation instead of over-weighting one personal scar.

notes.front: How does the book frame the boundary between architecture and design?
notes.back: As a spectrum, not a line. Strategic, hard-to-change, high-effort decisions lean architectural; tactical, easy-to-change decisions lean design. Architects and developers should collaborate continuously rather than throw decisions “over the wall.”
The degree to which the parts of a module belong together — how related and focused a module’s responsibilities are. High cohesion is desirable.
Afferent (incoming): number of components that depend on this component. Efferent (outgoing): number of components this component depends on.
Two components are connascent if a change in one would require the other to change to preserve overall correctness. Analysed by strength, locality, and degree.
Detectable by static source analysis: connascence of Name, Type, Meaning (Convention), Position, and Algorithm.
Detectable only at runtime: connascence of Execution (order), Timing, Values, and Identity. Dynamic connascence is generally worse than static.

notes.front: Three properties used to evaluate connascence?
notes.back:
• Strength — ease of refactoring (static is stronger / easier than dynamic).
  • Locality — how close the connascent elements are in the codebase.
  • Degree — the size of the impact / number of entities affected.

notes.front: Abstractness, Instability (I), and Distance from the Main Sequence (D)?
notes.back: Abstractness = ratio of abstract to concrete elements in a component. Instability I = Ce / (Ce + Ca) (efferent over total coupling). Distance D = |A + I − 1|; near 0 is a healthy balance.

From the abstractness/instability graph. Zone of pain: highly concrete and stable — rigid, hard to change. Zone of uselessness: highly abstract and unstable — abstractions nobody uses. Good components sit near the main sequence line between them.
The primary modular building block and unit of deployment — a library, package, service, or layer. It’s the lowest level of the system an architect typically manipulates directly.
An independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion and synchronous connascence. It measures partitioning: a monolith is one quantum; microservices form many quanta.
Static: how parts are wired together — dependencies, contracts, and infrastructure needed to operate. Dynamic: how parts communicate at runtime — synchronous vs asynchronous calls.

notes.front: Three criteria for something to be an architecture characteristic?
notes.back: It must (1) specify a non-domain design consideration, (2) influence some structural aspect of the design, and (3) be critical or important to the application’s success.

notes.front: Operational vs structural vs cross-cutting characteristics — examples?
notes.back:
• Operational: availability, performance, scalability, recoverability.
  • Structural: modularity, maintainability, configurability, extensibility.
  • Cross-cutting: security, accessibility, authentication, privacy.
Implicit: rarely written in requirements but almost always needed (availability, security, performance). Explicit: stated directly in the requirements.

notes.front: Why deliberately limit the number of characteristics you target?
notes.back: Each characteristic adds complexity and often conflicts with others; chasing too many yields a generic, over-engineered design. Guideline: “never shoot for the best architecture, but rather the least worst architecture.”

notes.front: How can architecture characteristics be measured (three categories)?
notes.back:
• Operational measures — e.g. response time, throughput, SLA targets.
  • Structural measures — e.g. cyclomatic complexity, coupling metrics.
  • Process measures — e.g. agility, deployability, testability tied to the dev process.

notes.front: What is a fitness function in architecture governance?
notes.back: Any objective, automatable check that assesses whether the architecture meets a desired characteristic — e.g. a test that fails when cyclomatic complexity exceeds a threshold, or one that enforces allowed layer dependencies. Enables continuous governance.

notes.front: Why are architecture characteristics often in conflict? Give an example.
notes.back: Optimising one frequently degrades another, so architects balance rather than maximise. Example: adding security checks/encryption usually reduces performance; maximising raw performance can hurt scalability or modularity.

Monolithic: a single deployment unit holding all code (layered, pipeline, microkernel). Distributed: multiple independently deployed units communicating over a network (service-based, event-driven, space-based, SOA, microservices).

• The network is reliable
  • Latency is zero
  • Bandwidth is infinite
  • The network is secure
  • Topology never changes
  • There is one administrator
  • Transport cost is zero
  • The network is homogeneous
The absence of any discernible architecture — tangled, highly coupled code with no clear structure, usually from unmanaged organic growth.
When requests pass through layers that add no logic — pure pass-through — so the layers add overhead without value. Watch the ~80/20 ratio of meaningful vs pass-through requests.
A closed layer must be traversed by any request moving down the stack, enforcing layers of isolation. An open layer may be bypassed. Isolation limits the blast radius of change.

notes.front: How does the book compare architecture styles? (the star system)
notes.back: Each style is scored ~1–5 stars across characteristics — deployability, elasticity, evolvability, fault tolerance, modularity, overall cost, performance, reliability, scalability, simplicity, testability — to compare tradeoffs rather than crown a single “best” style.

notes.front: Which characteristics push you from a monolith toward a distributed style?
notes.back: High scalability/elasticity, fault tolerance (failure isolation), independent deployability, and evolvability — accepting higher cost, operational complexity, and network performance overhead.

notes.front: Which architecture style is shown, and what are its layers?
notes.back: Layered (n-tier) architecture. Typical layers: presentation → business → persistence → database, each usually closed to enforce layers of isolation.

Strengths: simplicity, low cost, easy to build; a sensible default/starting point. Weaknesses: poor scalability, elasticity, fault tolerance, and deployability (it’s monolithic); prone to the architecture-sinkhole antipattern.
Pipeline (pipes and filters) architecture: self-contained, stateless filters connected by unidirectional pipes.

notes.front: Pipeline architecture — the four filter types?
notes.back:
• Producer (source) — start point.
  • Transformer — maps/changes data.
  • Tester — filters or branches based on a test.
  • Consumer (sink) — endpoint.
Filters are single-purpose, stateless, and independent.
Microkernel (plug-in) architecture: a minimal core system plus independent, decoupled plug-in components.

notes.front: Microkernel architecture — core idea and typical uses?
notes.back: A minimal core handles the basic flow; specialised or volatile logic lives in independent plug-ins. A registry tracks available plug-ins and contracts govern their communication. Common for product-based apps and tools (Integrated Development Environments / IDEs, browsers with extensions, insurance claims/rules engines).
Service-based architecture — a user interface calling a few coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services, typically over a shared database.

notes.front: Service-based architecture — defining traits and why it’s called “pragmatic”?
notes.back: A distributed macro-layered style: a UI calls a small set (often 4–12) of coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services, usually sharing one monolithic database. It delivers much of microservices’ benefit (deployability, fault isolation, evolvability) with far less complexity — hence the most pragmatic distributed architecture.

notes.front: Which architecture style is shown, and what are its two topologies?
notes.back: Event-driven architecture. Broker topology (no central coordinator) vs mediator topology (central event mediator).

Broker: no central coordinator; events broadcast in a chain, each processor reacts and emits more events — highly decoupled and performant, but workflow control and error handling are hard. Mediator: a central mediator orchestrates the steps — better error handling/recoverability, at the cost of more coupling and a potential bottleneck.

notes.front: Event-driven architecture — overall strengths and weaknesses?
notes.back: Strengths: excellent performance, scalability, elasticity, fault tolerance, responsiveness; highly decoupled. Weaknesses: low simplicity, hard to test, complex error handling, non-deterministic flows and eventual consistency.
Space-based architecture — processing units with replicated in-memory data grids over virtualized middleware, with asynchronous data pumps to the database.

notes.front: Space-based architecture — core idea, key parts, and when to use it?
notes.back: Named after tuple space / shared memory. Data lives in replicated in-memory data grids inside processing units, removing the central database bottleneck; the database is updated asynchronously via data pumps/writers. Parts: processing units, virtualized middleware (messaging / data / processing grids + deployment manager), data pumps, data writers/readers. Best for high, spiky, variable load (ticketing, auctions). Gives extreme scalability and elasticity.
Orchestration-driven Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) — a hierarchical service taxonomy mediated by a central orchestration engine / Enterprise Service Bus (ESB).

notes.front: Orchestration-driven SOA — the service taxonomy and why it fell out of favour?
notes.back: Hierarchical services: business (abstract, the “what”), enterprise (concrete, coarse-grained, reusable), application, and infrastructure services — mediated by a central orchestration engine / Enterprise Service Bus (ESB). Heavy reuse plus central mediation made systems brittle: one change rippled widely, killing evolvability. The book treats it as largely superseded.
Microservices architecture — fine-grained, single-purpose services, each owning its own data (share-nothing), behind an API layer/gateway.

Built on Domain-Driven Design’s bounded context: each service is fine-grained, single-purpose, owns its own data (share-nothing), is independently deployable, and communicates over the network (often via an API layer/gateway). Favour duplication over coupling.

Strengths: best-in-class deployability, evolvability, testability, scalability, elasticity, and fault tolerance. Weaknesses: poor performance (network hops + per-call security), low simplicity, high cost and operational complexity, and full distributed-systems difficulty (the 8 fallacies, distributed transactions).

notes.front: Why is simplicity rated high for layered/microkernel but low for microservices?
notes.back: Monolithic styles have no network, no distributed data, and few moving parts — easy to reason about and operate. Microservices add distribution, many deployment units, and operational tooling, sharply lowering simplicity.

notes.front: Bounded context (Domain-Driven Design) — and why microservices embrace it?
notes.back: A model and its data are valid only within an explicit boundary; each context owns its own representation. Microservices map one service per bounded context so each owns its data and avoids shared-data coupling.

Choreography (broker-style, decentralised): services react to events — better decoupling and scaling. Orchestration: a coordinator/mediator drives the workflow — easier complex error handling and workflow control, but more coupling.

notes.front: Sidecar pattern and service mesh (microservices operational concern)?
notes.back: Cross-cutting operational concerns (monitoring, logging, service discovery, security) are factored into a sidecar deployed beside each service; the collection of sidecars forms a service mesh, giving consistent infrastructure without coupling business code.

A way to keep data consistent across services without distributed Atomicity-Consistency-Isolation-Durability (ACID) transactions: a sequence of local transactions, each triggering the next, with compensating transactions to undo work on failure.
A short document capturing a single architecture decision — typically title, status, context, decision, consequences. ADRs preserve the “why” (Second Law) and build a durable, reviewable history.

notes.front: The four levels of the C4 diagramming model?
notes.back: Context, Container, Component, Code — four levels of zoom. Pair with consistent notation, clear legends, and labelled lines. Diagramming and presenting are core architect communication skills.

notes.front: Risk matrix for architecture risk analysis?
notes.back: Rate each risk on two axes — likelihood (low/medium/high) and impact (low/medium/high) — forming a 3×3 grid; the product surfaces high-priority (high/high) risks for attention.
A collaborative exercise where several participants independently identify and rate risks on an architecture diagram, then converge — surfacing risks a single architect would miss.

notes.front: Conway’s Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver?
notes.back: Conway’s Law: organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structures. The Inverse Conway Maneuver deliberately restructures teams to encourage a desired architecture (e.g. one team per service).

notes.front: How do team boundaries relate to architecture (Team Topologies idea)?
notes.back: Because team structure and system structure mirror each other (Conway’s Law), architects should design boundaries — such as a service per team — so communication paths match the desired architecture, and lead with elastic, context-appropriate control.

notes.front: Why does “there are no right or wrong answers in architecture, only expensive ones” fit the book?
notes.back: Because everything is a tradeoff (First Law). Decisions aren’t right/wrong in the abstract — they carry costs and consequences that must be weighed against the required characteristics.

notes.front: What does it mean that architecture is iterative / evolutionary?
notes.back: Decisions and characteristics are refined as understanding grows rather than fully specified up front. Supported by evolutionary architecture and automated fitness functions for ongoing governance.
